newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Supply may hamper U.S. but not Spain.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Supply may hamper U.S. but not Spain.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries may not find it easy to absorb supply in the short term, but Spanish government auctions are expected to fare better, analysts said on Wednesday.

In Britain some analysts said the Bank of England might take advantage of Tuesday's rally and the flatness of the yield curve to issue 10-year paper, but others did not see the economic backdrop favouring such a move.
"The broad picture remains one of buoyant growth in the U.S. and UK and on the back of that yields will be in an upward trending environment," said Kirit Shah, at Sanwa International in London.

"It is going to be very difficult to tap new issuance," Shah, Sanwa's chief international strategist, said adding that in the U.S. recent hectic corporate issuance would also hamper Treasuries' struggle to make new ground.

Analysts said the result of Tuesday's auction of $17 billion of three-year notes had been disappointing, but expected greater interest in the $12.0 billion 10-year notes to be auctioned later in the session.
David Hewitt, bond strategist at Tokyo Mitsubishi, in London, said there were two conflicting factors which might affect the auction looking back to the last auction in February.
"In moving from November to February the yield drop was four basis points but this time the roll is positive, so you are getting a yield pick-up on moving into the new bond," he said.
However against this he said prices had fallen considerably since the February auction.

"A lot of people will be reluctant to realise that loss even though they are getting a bit of a pick-up in yield. They might hold onto the old bond," said Hewitt. "It is not entirely certain given that and given the flat curve whether we will see significant cover this time."
But on a medium to long-term view some analysts were more positive on U.S. Treasuries.
Steve Major, head of bond research in London, said much of the risk from bond negative data was already priced into the market.

"The general overview is that the auction is not enough to hold the market back," he said. "It is not a big problem for the market to absorb because the background of the budget negotiations is fairly positive, and with tightening largely discounted in the Eurodollar curve."
Major said the key factors were that the U.S. was heading towards a balanced budget and the market had discounted three sets of rate tightening up to the end of the year.
"With the market pricing in 75 basis points of tightening already, rates will have to be a lot higher to make the market negative," he said.
Many in the market are expecting a rate cut after the Federal Open Market Committee meeting on May 20.
Elsewhere, Spain is currently in the second day of government bond auctions and Italy is to detail its mid-month auction.

"Spain seems to be going well, buoyed by the rate cut expectations for next week," said Major. "There is a good chance Spain will cut rates after the inflation data. It has a strong budget position and a strong currency so everything is in place."

In Britain, Shah said the spread between five and 10-year gilts was around 14 basis points giving investors incentive to shorten duration risk. After Tuesday's steep rally, the Bank of England might be encouraged to tap the market, he said.

"You normally get such a tight spread at the top of a tightening cycle when the market considers inflation has peaked," he said. "From a borrowers perspective the Bank of England should come in in the 10-year sector and borrow the long end."
